A Sipping Rum Guide for Anyone Starting From Scratch

Rum is the most varied spirit category in existence and the least well explained. Whisky drinkers can rely on region and age statement to tell them roughly what is in the bottle. Rum offers no such comfort. Two bottles side by side, both labelled rum, both aged, both from the Caribbean, can be as different as vodka and Islay whisky.

That variety is exactly what makes it rewarding once you have a few reference points. This sipping rum guide is about establishing those points, so that you can walk past a shelf and make a sensible guess at what is inside.

Everything Starts With the Still

The single most useful thing to know about a rum is what kind of still it came out of. Column stills run continuously and produce a light, clean, high-strength spirit with relatively little flavour carried over. Pot stills work in batches, are far less efficient at stripping out the heavier compounds, and produce a spirit thick with flavour: overripe fruit, banana, olive brine, engine oil, tropical funk.

Neither is better. Column-still rum is the backbone of most mixing rum and of the lighter Spanish-influenced styles, and made well it is elegant. Pot-still rum is where the intensity lives, and it is generally what you want if you are drinking neat.

Most of the best sipping rums are blends of the two, using column spirit for structure and pot spirit for character. If a label mentions pot still at all, it is telling you something useful. If it says nothing, assume column.

Age Statements Mean Something Different Here

Tropical heat changes everything about maturation. Spirit resting in a warehouse in Barbados or Jamaica interacts with oak far more aggressively than the same spirit would in Scotland, and it evaporates at roughly three to four times the rate. A Caribbean warehouse can lose 6 to 8 per cent of its volume a year against about 2 per cent in a Scottish one.

The practical consequence is that a six or seven year old tropically aged rum often has the depth of a considerably older northern-aged whisky, and that very old rums are genuinely rare and expensive because so little survives. Do not dismiss a rum for being young.

Be cautious with two labelling practices. A solera age statement usually refers to the oldest component in a blend rather than the youngest, which is the opposite of how whisky works. And a number on a bottle with no unit attached is sometimes a batch or recipe number rather than an age. If the label does not say years, it may well not mean years.

The Sugar Question

Unlike Scotch, most rum-producing regions permit sweetening after distillation, and a number of well-known bottlings contain a meaningful amount of added sugar. It is legal and it is not a scandal, but it does matter to a beginner, because sugar rounds off edges and makes a spirit taste smoother, richer and older than it is.

The problem for learning is that it flattens the differences you are trying to detect. If your first three rums are all heavily sweetened, they will all taste broadly similar and you will conclude that rum is a fairly narrow category.

Look for producers who state that nothing has been added after distillation. Rums from Barbados, Jamaica and the French islands are generally unsweetened by tradition or regulation, and they are the best place to begin building a palate.

The Regional Styles Worth Knowing

Jamaica is the home of high-ester rum, with pronounced overripe banana, pineapple and a distinctive funk that comes from long fermentation. It is polarising and it is the fastest way to discover whether you like pot-still character.

Barbados sits in the middle and is probably the best starting point of all. Blended pot and column rums with toffee, banana, toasted coconut and a clean finish, dry rather than sweet, and rarely difficult.

Guyana produces the Demerara style from a famous collection of wooden stills, giving a rich, smoky, treacle-and-liquorice profile that stands up to anything.

The Spanish-speaking tradition, covering Cuba, Panama, Venezuela and much of Central America, favours lighter column-still rums, often softer and sweeter, and generally more approachable but less distinctive.

Martinique and Guadeloupe make rhum agricole from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, which produces a grassy, vegetal, almost peppery spirit unlike anything else in the category. It divides opinion sharply and is worth trying early so you know where you stand.

You will find examples of several of these traditions in the spirits range.

How to Actually Taste It

Use a copita or a small tulip-shaped glass rather than a heavy tumbler. A wide-mouthed glass lets aroma escape, and rum is a spirit where aroma carries most of the interest.

Serve at room temperature to begin with, no ice. Cold suppresses the fruit and the oak notes you are trying to identify. Nose it gently with your mouth slightly open, and do not stick your nose deep into the glass, since the alcohol vapour will overwhelm everything else.

Take a small sip and let it sit on the tongue before swallowing. Then add two or three drops of still water and taste it again. Water lowers the alcohol strength enough to release aromatic compounds, and the difference is often dramatic, particularly with anything bottled above 46 per cent.

Only after all of that should you try it with a single large ice cube, if you want to. A big cube dilutes slowly, which is exactly what you want in a spirit you intend to spend half an hour with.

Building a First Shelf

Three bottles will teach you more than any amount of reading. Start with a Barbadian blend as your reference point, add a Jamaican pot-still rum to understand what ester character means, and add a Demerara for richness and depth. Taste them side by side in small measures rather than working through one bottle at a time, because the contrasts are what teach you.

Add an agricole fourth if the first three have gone well, and expect to either love it or find it baffling. Both reactions are common and neither is wrong.

Can You Get Alcohol Delivered at 3am in London? Yes — Here's How It Works

Yes. Drinks House 247 delivers alcohol across London 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and an order placed at 3am is handled exactly like one placed at 3pm — typically arriving within 30 to 45 minutes inside the M25. The person who takes the delivery must be 18 or over and may be asked for photo ID.

Most people discover overnight delivery at the worst possible moment: the party is still going, the shops shut hours ago, and the nearest 24-hour garage sells crisps and nothing stronger. This page explains what actually happens when you order in the middle of the night, what the law allows, and how long you should realistically expect to wait.

How does 3am alcohol delivery actually work?

You order online exactly as you would at any other hour. Payment is taken at checkout — card, Apple Pay, Google Pay or PayPal — and the order goes straight to a driver working the night shift. Drivers run from our Battersea base and cover every London borough inside the M25.

There is no separate night-time process, no callback to confirm, and no minimum you have to reach before anyone will come out. The only meaningful difference between a 3am order and a 3pm one is that the roads are emptier.

Is it legal to buy alcohol at 3am in the UK?

It is legal where the retailer holds a licence permitting sales at that hour. Under the Licensing Act 2003, the sale is treated as concluded when the order is accepted, and a licensed retailer whose premises licence covers 24-hour sales can take and fulfil orders through the night.

This is why delivery and shops diverge after midnight. Most off-licences in London are licensed to stop selling somewhere between 11pm and 1am, so the shutters come down. A licensed delivery service operating under its own premises licence is not bound by another shop's hours, which is why delivery is often the only option available at 3am.

What does not change at any hour is the age requirement. Selling or delivering alcohol to anyone under 18 is an offence regardless of the time, and no responsible retailer will make an exception because it is late.

What will the driver ask for at the door?

We operate a Challenge 25 policy. If whoever answers the door looks under 25, the driver will ask for photo ID — a passport, a UK driving licence, or a PASS-accredited card. If nobody present can produce acceptable ID, the driver cannot hand the order over. That rule holds at 3am exactly as it does at 3pm.

Alcohol also cannot be left on a doorstep, with a neighbour, or in a safe place, because the age check has to happen in person. Put a working mobile number on the order so the driver can reach you if the buzzer is broken or the building entrance is confusing — at night, that one detail prevents most failed deliveries.

Which parts of London are covered overnight?

Same-day and overnight delivery covers every borough inside the M25, from Mayfair, Soho and Chelsea in the centre to Canary Wharf, Camden, Clapham, Greenwich, Ealing and Croydon further out. Central and inner London tends to sit at the shorter end of the 30 to 45 minute range; the outer edges of the M25 take longer simply because of distance. You can check your area on our delivery areas page.

Outside London, orders are sent next day to UK mainland addresses by courier, so overnight delivery is a London service rather than a national one.

What can you order in the middle of the night?

The full range, not a reduced late-night selection. That includes champagne, wine, spirits, beer and mixers, along with the gift lines. Late orders skew heavily towards champagne and spirits, which makes sense — nobody is doing their weekly shop at 3am, they are topping up a celebration that has outlasted its supplies.

If you are sending to someone else at that hour, enter their address at checkout rather than your own, and be aware that whoever opens the door still has to be over 18.

Alcohol Delivery to London Offices: How It Works

Yes, alcohol can be delivered to a London office, and it is one of the most common business requests we handle. Drinks House 247 delivers across every borough inside the M25, usually within 30 to 45 minutes. Whoever signs for the order — including a receptionist or post-room staff — must be 18 or over and may be asked for photo ID.

Office deliveries fail for boring reasons: no named recipient, a locked lobby, or a driver arriving at 1pm when the whole floor is at lunch. Here is how to get it right.

What to put on the delivery address

Office buildings route deliveries by name, not by order number. Include the recipient's full name, the company name, and the floor or suite. In multi-tenant buildings the company name matters more than anything else — reception will not know who the order belongs to without it.

Always add a mobile number. Lobby intercoms fail, security desks turn drivers away, and a working phone number resolves both in under a minute. This single field prevents most failed office deliveries.

Who can legally sign for it?

Anyone over 18 who is present to receive it. That includes reception staff, a post room, or a colleague — it does not have to be the person named on the order. We operate a Challenge 25 policy, so if whoever accepts the delivery looks under 25, the driver will ask for photo ID.

What cannot happen is the order being left unattended at a desk or in a mail room with nobody signing. The age check has to happen in person, which is the one part of the process that is not negotiable.

Team celebration 3pm–5pm Order early; Friday afternoons are the busiest slot

The one window to avoid is 12.30pm to 2pm. Reception is thinly staffed, the named recipient is out, and a delivery that would take two minutes at 10am turns into a redelivery.

Bulk and case orders

Office parties and large team events are usually easier as case orders than as individual bottles — fewer items to check in at reception, and easier to store. Think about what the office can actually chill: a case of champagne is no use at 4pm if there is one under-counter fridge.

For larger orders it is worth planning around two weeks ahead so quantities can be confirmed, though same-day delivery in London means genuine last-minute top-ups remain possible. See office party alcohol delivery for bulk options.

Sending to a client's office

Corporate gifting has one rule that differs from personal gifting: the recipient may not be there, and the gift may sit in a post room over a weekend. That argues for bottles rather than anything perishable, and for presentation that survives being handled.

Add a gift note at checkout so the recipient knows who it is from — an unlabelled bottle arriving at a busy office is a wasted gesture. Browse gift sets and hampers or corporate alcohol gifts.

It is also worth a moment's thought about the recipient. Some companies have policies capping the value of gifts staff may accept, and some clients do not drink. Neither is a reason to avoid sending alcohol, but both are reasons to know your recipient before you do.

Every borough inside the M25, which covers the City, Canary Wharf, Mayfair, Soho, Shoreditch, Victoria, King's Cross and the rest of the commercial centre. Central and inner London sits at the shorter end of the 30 to 45 minute range. Check your postcode on our delivery areas page. Offices outside London are served next day to UK mainland addresses.

Staying Safe and Responsible with Alcohol Delivery

Staying safe and responsible is crucial when using alcoholic beverage delivery services in the UK. Ensuring only adults receive alcoholic beverage delivery is a legal requirement. Providers must follow strict age verification, typically using the Challenge 25 policy. This means drivers are trained to request valid photo ID from anyone who appears under 25.

The late summer bank holiday lands on Monday 31 August 2026, which means a three-day weekend starting Saturday 29 August, and for a lot of people it is the last proper outdoor weekend of the year. It is also the weekend when supermarket shelves get stripped, corner shops sell out of ice by lunchtime on Sunday, and somebody ends up making a supply run at nine in the evening.

Getting bank holiday drinks right is mostly about ordering the correct proportions rather than the correct brands. Here is how to work out what you actually need, and what genuinely works across a long, warm, three-day weekend.

Work out the quantities before anything else

The most common mistake is buying a wide range of exciting things and not enough of the boring reliable ones. For a daytime gathering of adults running four to five hours, plan on roughly four to five drinks per head across the whole event, and weight the mix heavily towards lower-strength options.

For twelve people, a solid baseline is two cases of beer or cider, four bottles of wine split across white, rose and a light red, one bottle of spirit with mixers, and at least twice as much soft drink and water as you think anyone will touch. If the party runs into the evening, add a case of beer rather than another bottle of spirits, because people slow down as it gets later and spirits at nine at night is how a good day ends early.

Ice is the one thing almost everybody underestimates. Buy or make roughly a kilo per person for a warm day. It goes into drinks, into the cool box and into the sink where you are chilling bottles, and there is never enough.

The beer and cider order

Cold, crisp and moderate is the brief. Pale lager is unbeatable at a barbecue because it cuts through smoke and fat and resets the palate between mouthfuls, and at four to five percent people can drink it across an afternoon without falling over. Dry cider does much the same job and is a useful option for anyone who does not like beer.

Buy cans over bottles for anything happening outdoors. They chill faster, they stack better in a cool box, they do not shatter on a patio and they are easier to clear up. Keep any bottles for the kitchen. Have a look at the beer range and pick two styles rather than six, since variety matters far less than everything being properly cold.

On chilling: a cool box with ice and water chills warm cans in about twenty minutes, whereas ice alone takes over an hour. Water conducts heat away far faster than air does. That single trick saves the day when guests arrive early.

Wine for a warm afternoon

Heat changes what works. Big oaky whites and heavy reds both fall apart in the sun, going flabby and alcoholic. What you want is acidity.

For whites, choose something crisp and dry with real freshness. For rose, dry rather than sweet, and serve it as cold as a white. For red, this is the moment for a light, juicy style served with twenty minutes in the fridge first. A chilled light red at a barbecue is one of the most underrated drinks of the British summer and converts almost everyone who tries it.

Serve white and rose at 8 to 10 degrees and top up the ice bucket regularly, because a bottle left on a table in the sun is at room temperature within fifteen minutes. Browse the wine range and buy one more bottle of white than you think you need, since white and rose always go faster than red on a warm day.

One jug, made in advance

Do not stand at a table building individual cocktails for twelve people. Make one large batch of something long and relatively low in strength, put it in the fridge in the morning, and only add ice when you serve it so it does not water down while it waits.

The format that works is roughly one part spirit to three parts juice or soft mixer, plus fresh citrus, chilled hard and served over plenty of ice with fruit floated on top. Gin with cloudy apple juice and lemon, vodka with grapefruit and soda, or a white wine spritz with sparkling water and cucumber all scale beautifully and none of them require anyone to stand behind a shaker. A bottle from the spirits selection goes much further this way than poured neat over ice.

Something for the moment it turns into an evening

Bank holiday Sundays have a habit of turning into evenings without anyone deciding they should. Keep one bottle of fizz in the fridge, whether that is prosecco or something from the champagne range, plus a bottle of decent red for whoever is still there when it gets cold and someone puts the oven on.

Also keep a proper non-alcoholic option that is not just lemonade. Cold soda with plenty of lime and mint, or a jug of iced tea, means the people who are driving or not drinking are not stuck with warm cola all afternoon.

Timing your order

Order before the Saturday if you can. The whole country is doing the same thing that weekend, delivery slots elsewhere fill up, and shops near anywhere popular get thin on stock by Sunday afternoon. An Autumn Wine Guide for the Turn of the Season

The standard autumn wine guide tells you to switch to red and leaves it there, which is not much use in the first week of September when it is still fifteen degrees at six in the evening. The real change is more gradual and more interesting than that, and it is driven less by temperature than by what you are eating.

Summer food is light, acidic and often cold. Autumn food is roasted, braised, earthy and served hot. Wine follows the plate, not the calendar, so the useful question is not whether it is autumn yet but what is coming out of your oven.

Do Not Abandon White Wine, Change Its Style

The most common mistake is packing the white wine away in September. What actually needs to change is the type of white you are drinking.

Summer whites are lean and high in acid, built to refresh: Pinot Grigio, Picpoul, unoaked Sauvignon Blanc. Autumn whites want texture and weight instead. Oaked Chardonnay from Burgundy or a good New World producer is the obvious one, but Chenin Blanc from the Loire or South Africa is arguably better value, with honeyed weight and enough acidity to cut through richness. Viognier brings apricot and a fuller body. Aged white Rioja, which spends time in oak, is one of the great underrated autumn wines and costs a fraction of white Burgundy.

These all suit exactly what you start cooking in September: roast chicken, mushrooms, squash, leeks, anything with cream or butter. Browse the full wine range and look at the whites before you write them off for the year.

Early Autumn Reds: Medium Bodied and Chilled

September and early October belong to the middle of the red spectrum. You want fruit, freshness and moderate tannin, not weight.

Gamay, in the form of Beaujolais, is close to perfect here. Cru Beaujolais such as Fleurie, Morgon or Brouilly gives you real structure without heaviness, and it can be served lightly chilled, which matters when the weather has not fully committed. Pinot Noir does the same job with more earth and less bright fruit. Barbera from Piedmont has high acidity and low tannin, which makes it the most food-friendly red on the shelf and remarkably good with tomato-based dishes and with sausages.

All three benefit from twenty minutes in the fridge. Lightly chilled red is standard practice across most of wine-producing Europe and a persistent blind spot in Britain.

Later Autumn: Bringing Out the Weight

By late October and November, the food has changed again and heavier wines start to make sense. This is when Rioja Reserva, Rhone Syrah, Malbec and Cabernet blends come into their own, alongside slow-cooked meat, game and root vegetables.

The pairing logic is simple enough. Tannin binds with protein and fat, so a tannic red that tastes harsh on its own becomes soft and generous alongside a piece of beef or a lamb shoulder. That is why the same bottle can seem impressive at dinner and unpleasant on the sofa afterwards.

If you are buying reds to keep for the season, the red wine collection is the place to start.

The Temperature Problem

More autumn wine is spoiled by serving temperature than by any other single factor, and it costs nothing to fix.

Room temperature as a guideline dates from an era of unheated stone houses, where a room might be fifteen degrees. A modern British living room in November sits at twenty-one or higher, and at that temperature alcohol becomes dominant, fruit flattens out and tannin turns coarse. Most reds show best between fifteen and eighteen degrees, and lighter styles nearer thirteen.

The practical version: put red wine in the fridge for twenty minutes before you open it. Take white wine out of the fridge twenty minutes before you pour it, because most people serve white far too cold, which mutes aroma entirely. Those two habits will improve your wine drinking more than spending an extra five pounds a bottle.

Decanting, and When It Actually Helps

Decanting has a reputation for fussiness it does not deserve. It does two things: it removes sediment from older bottles, and it exposes young wine to oxygen, which softens tannin and opens up aroma.

The second is the one that matters for most autumn drinking. A young, tannic red under about ten years old benefits from thirty to sixty minutes in a decanter, or simply from being poured into a jug and back into the bottle if you do not own one. Older wines, over about fifteen years, are fragile and should be opened and poured carefully rather than aerated aggressively.

Buying for the Season Rather Than the Night

Autumn is the point in the year when it becomes worth keeping a small spread of wine at home rather than buying bottle by bottle. Six bottles covering three price points and both colours will handle almost anything that comes up: an unexpected dinner, a Sunday roast, a cold Tuesday evening.

Store them somewhere cool and dark and away from the kitchen, which is the warmest room in most flats and the worst place for a wine rack. A cupboard on an outside wall beats a shelf above the oven every time.

Start With Something Cold and Sparkling

An arrival drink does a lot of work. It gives people something to hold while they find their feet, and it sets the tone before anyone has decided what they actually want. Champagne is the obvious choice for a milestone, but prosecco does the same job at a friendlier price when you are pouring for twenty people. Either way, keep bottles in ice rather than out on a table. Sparkling wine warms up faster than still wine and loses its appeal quickly once it does.

Chilled Whites and Rose Do the Heavy Lifting

Through the afternoon, most people gravitate to something light and cold. Crisp whites such as Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and unoaked Chardonnay all work well in the heat, as does dry rose, which has the useful quality of appealing to both white and red drinkers.

Red wine is worth having, but keep it to a bottle or two of something lighter rather than a heavy, high-alcohol style. If you do serve red on a hot day, twenty minutes in the fridge before pouring makes an enormous difference. Browse the full wine range if you want to build a mixed selection.

Beer and Cider for the Long Haul

Beer is the drink people return to across a long, warm afternoon, and it is the one most often underestimated. Lagers such as Peroni, Corona, Stella Artois and Heineken suit garden drinking better than heavier ales, and cider is worth including for anyone who wants something cold and less bitter.

The practical point is chilling. Beer needs to be genuinely cold, not merely cool, and a fridge full of bottles takes a couple of hours to get there. If you are running short on time or space, a bucket of ice and water chills faster than ice alone. Stock up from the beer collection.

One Batched Cocktail, Not Six

Cocktails are a lovely idea and a terrible plan if you are making them to order. The fix is to batch one drink in a jug or dispenser and let people help themselves. Something more thoughtful than warm lemonade matters more than most hosts expect. Designated drivers, guests who are not drinking, and anyone pacing themselves in the heat will all thank you. Choosing Drinks for Watching Sport at Home

Choosing drinks for watching sport looks like a simple question and is actually a scheduling one. The variable that matters most is not what sport you are watching, it is how long you will be sitting there and what time it starts. Here is how we would think about it, sport by sport and hour by hour.

Work Out the Length First

Everything follows from duration. A football match is roughly two hours door to door once you factor in build-up and analysis. A rugby international is similar. A cricket day is seven hours. A Grand Prix with the pre-race show is three. A boxing undercard can run five hours before the main event walks out.

For anything under two hours, strength barely matters and you can drink whatever you actually enjoy. Beyond three hours, alcohol by volume becomes the whole game. Dropping from a five per cent lager to a four per cent one across a long afternoon is the difference between remembering the second half and not.

The Ninety-Minute Match: Cold and Crisp

For a single game, you want something cold, clean and easy to drink between moments of shouting at a television. Crisp lagers are the default for a reason. Asahi and Peroni are dry and refreshing without much bitterness, Heineken and Stella Artois are the familiar middle ground, and Corona with a lime is the choice when the weather is still warm.

Two practical notes. Serve from a bottle or can rather than pouring into a glass you then have to keep refilling in the middle of an attacking move. And chill more than you plan to drink, because a warm second beer ruins the pattern. The beer range covers most of the usual suspects.

The All-Day Tournament: Pace Yourself Deliberately

Test cricket, a full Six Nations Saturday, a golf major, a race weekend. These are endurance events and the mistake everyone makes is drinking at match-day pace from the first session.

Three tactics work. First, go lower in strength from the outset rather than switching later, when it feels like a downgrade. Second, build long drinks with plenty of ice and mixer rather than serving anything neat. A tall gin and tonic or a rum and ginger over a full glass of ice takes twenty minutes to finish and hydrates you slightly as it goes. Third, put a jug of iced water on the table at the start, not once someone thinks to ask.

Cider is underrated here too. It is refreshing, generally a little lower in strength than craft beer, and it suits a long slow afternoon in a way that a heavily hopped IPA does not.

Late Nights and Odd Hours

Overnight boxing, an Australian Test, a Grand Prix from the other side of the world. These change the calculation entirely, because you are drinking against your body clock rather than with it.

Volume is the enemy. One or two considered drinks beat a case of lager at three in the morning, and this is the one situation where a good whisky genuinely earns its place. A single measure, no ice or one large cube, sipped slowly across a couple of rounds, keeps you sharp in a way that six beers will not. A stout works on the same principle: rich enough to be satisfying, slow enough to last. Have a look at the spirits range if you are building a late-night setup.

Feeding People Without Missing Anything

Snacks and drinks interact more than people expect. Salt drives drinking, and a bowl of crisps put out at kick-off will roughly double the rate at which the first round disappears. That is fine if you have planned for it and a problem if you have not.

Put the food out at half time rather than the start, keep it in reach of the sofa so nobody has to move, and choose things that survive an hour on a table. And if you are hosting a mixed group, batch one thing in a jug before the start so nobody is standing at a worktop building drinks while a penalty is being taken.

The Big Occasion: Something to Toast With

Cup finals, title deciders and last-day promotion scrambles deserve a bottle standing by. There is no better use for a bottle of fizz than opening it the moment the whistle goes, and no worse feeling than realising you have nothing to open.

Keep it cold from the start rather than optimistically putting it in the freezer at the eighty-minute mark. A bottle of champagne or prosecco in the fridge costs nothing if the result goes the wrong way, and it can wait for another week.

The Best Gin Brands to Try This Year, Grouped by What They Actually Taste Like

There are now several hundred gins available in Britain, and the vast majority of them are variations on four or five underlying ideas. Lists of the best gin brands tend to be unhelpful because they rank bottles that are not trying to do the same thing, which is a bit like ranking a saw against a hammer.

The more useful approach is to work out which style you want, then pick a well-made example of it. Here are the categories that matter, what defines each one, and the names that are worth your attention within them.

The Classic Juniper-Led London Dry

This is the reference category, and every other style is defined by how far it departs from it. Expect dry pine, a citrus lift from lemon and orange peel in the still, and coriander seed providing a slightly spicy, aromatic backbone.

Tanqueray and Beefeater are the two most widely available benchmarks, both juniper-forward, both dry, both entirely reliable in a gin and tonic or a Negroni. Sipsmith brought the small-batch London Dry style back into the mainstream and is a touch softer and rounder. Tanqueray No. Ten is the same house at higher strength with fresh citrus in the still, and it makes a noticeably better Martini than most.

If you are buying one gin, buy from this group. They do everything, they are forgiving with cheap tonic, and they are the standard against which you will judge everything else you try.

Citrus-Forward Gins

These push lemon, grapefruit and sometimes bergamot to the front while keeping juniper present but less dominant. They are excellent in long drinks, in anything with a sour element, and for people who find classic gin too austere.

Malfy from Italy is built explicitly around lemon and blood orange and is unashamedly fruity. Tanqueray No. Ten again fits here as the more restrained option. Bombay Sapphire sits between citrus and floral and is milder than its reputation suggests, which makes it very approachable but easily overwhelmed by a strongly flavoured tonic.

The mistake with this category is over-garnishing. A citrus gin plus a slice of lemon plus a lemon tonic produces a drink that has lost all its structure. Use orange peel instead and let the gin do the work.

Floral and Contemporary Styles

This is where the modern gin boom really happened. These gins push juniper into a supporting role and build around roses, cucumber, elderflower, chamomile or lavender.

Hendrick s is the definitive example, with cucumber and rose giving a soft, perfumed character that converted an enormous number of people to gin. Gin Mare from Spain takes the same idea in a Mediterranean direction with olive, rosemary, thyme and basil, and it makes an unusual, savoury Martini that is worth trying at least once.

These gins reward careful serving. They are easily flattened by aggressive tonic, so use a plain Indian tonic rather than anything flavoured, and garnish lightly with cucumber or a strip of lime peel rather than lemon.

Spiced and Botanical-Heavy Gins

At the intense end of the shelf sit gins with large botanical counts and pronounced warm spice. Monkey 47 from the Black Forest uses forty seven botanicals and is dense, complex and slightly medicinal, with cranberry and pepper alongside the juniper. It is a gin to sip and to think about rather than to pour casually.

Roku from Japan is the gentler proposition in this group, built around six Japanese botanicals including sakura flower, yuzu peel and sencha tea, giving a delicate, layered character that is very different from European gin without being difficult.

Both are better served with less tonic than you would use for a classic gin, since the botanicals need room rather than dilution.

Navy Strength, and Why Strength Matters

Navy strength means 57 per cent alcohol or above, a designation with genuine historical roots in the Royal Navy. The point is not machismo. Higher strength carries aromatic compounds more effectively and stands up to dilution, which is exactly what you want in a drink built over ice or shaken with citrus.

Plymouth Navy Strength is the traditional example and is unexpectedly balanced for its strength. Any navy strength gin will transform a gin and tonic that has been tasting weak, because the problem was almost certainly dilution rather than the gin itself.

More generally, bottling strength is the most underrated number on a gin label. A 37.5 per cent gin will disappear in a long drink no matter how good the botanicals are. Forty per cent is workable, 43 to 47 per cent is the sweet spot for mixing.

How to Build a Gin Shelf Worth Having

Two bottles cover almost everyone. Start with a classic London Dry, which handles every standard drink. Then add one contrasting bottle in whichever direction interests you, whether that is citrus, floral or spiced. Those two will give you genuine variety without duplication.

Add navy strength third if you make cocktails regularly, and a Japanese or Mediterranean gin fourth if you have found that you enjoy exploring rather than repeating.

Taste anything new neat at room temperature before you mix it. Two minutes with a small measure in a wine glass tells you more about what you have bought than a whole evening of gin and tonics, because tonic flattens the differences you are paying for. The food is better, the weather is more forgiving, and the wines that suit this part of the year are more interesting than the pale, whisper-light bottles that dominate high summer.

Choosing the best rose wine for summer drinking is mostly a question of matching style to circumstance, and there are far more styles than the shelf layout suggests. Here is how the main ones actually differ, and what to do with them.

Provence, and Why Pale Is Not the Same as Good

Provence set the template for modern rose: pale onion skin or barely-there salmon, dry, low in obvious fruit, built around delicacy and a saline finish. At its best it is genuinely accomplished wine, refreshing without being simple, and it works beautifully as an aperitif before anyone has thought about food.

The problem is that pallor became a marketing shortcut. A great many producers now bleach the colour out of ordinary wine to make it look expensive, and the results are thin and forgettable. Colour in rose comes from skin contact time and grape variety, not from quality, so treat pale as a stylistic signal rather than a promise. Grenache-led blends with a little Cinsault and Syrah tend to give the most satisfying results. If a Provence rose smells of almost nothing in the glass, it will taste of almost nothing too, however chic the bottle.

Tavel and Bandol: Rose With Something to Say

These two southern French appellations make the roses worth reaching for in late summer, when you want something that can stand up to grilled food and a slight chill in the air.

Tavel, from the southern Rhone, is deliberately deep in colour, made from Grenache with Cinsault and Clairette, and has real weight without any sweetness. It handles lamb, charcuterie, anything charred and anything with garlic in it. Serve it a touch warmer than you would a pale rose, around 11 degrees, and it behaves almost like a very light red.

Bandol rose, built on Mourvedre, is the more serious proposition. It has a savoury, slightly herbal, faintly smoky character and a texture you can chew on. It also ages, which almost no other rose does convincingly. A three or four year old Bandol will taste more complex than the current vintage, not less.

Spain, Italy and the Underrated Middle Ground

Spanish rosado, particularly from Navarra and Rioja, is one of the great value categories in wine. Garnacha rosado gives strawberry and blood orange fruit with plenty of body, and prices remain sensible because the style has never been fashionable in the way Provence has. It is an excellent choice for a large gathering where you want the wine to be good rather than merely correct.

Italy offers rosato from Puglia, Abruzzo and Sicily with darker cherry fruit and a bitter almond twist on the finish that makes it unusually food-friendly. Cerasuolo d Abruzzo, made from Montepulciano, is worth seeking out and pairs remarkably well with tomato-based dishes that defeat most white wines.

English rose has improved dramatically, and sparkling English rose in particular has become a genuine alternative to pink Champagne, with sharper acidity and red fruit that reads as redcurrant rather than strawberry. You will find both still and sparkling styles alongside the rest of the wine range.

How Rose Is Actually Made, and Why It Matters

Two methods dominate. Direct press treats red grapes almost like white ones, crushing and pressing quickly so the juice picks up only a little colour. This gives the pale, delicate, aromatic style associated with Provence.

The saignee method bleeds off a portion of juice from a vat of red wine after a few hours of skin contact. The rose is a by-product of concentrating the red, and it tends to be darker, fruitier and fuller. Neither method is better, but knowing which you are drinking explains a great deal about what is in the glass. A wine that tastes surprisingly substantial for a rose has usually had more skin contact, whatever the label says about elegance.

Serving It Properly Makes More Difference Than the Label

Most rose in Britain is drunk far too cold. At 4 degrees straight from the fridge, aroma is suppressed and everything tastes of cold acidity. Fifteen minutes on the worktop before pouring transforms an average bottle. Aim for 8 to 10 degrees for pale styles and 10 to 12 for Tavel, Bandol and darker rosados.

Use a proper white wine glass rather than a tumbler or a small flute. Rose needs air and a bowl to develop aroma, and it is one of the wines most obviously improved by decent glassware. Once opened, a rose keeps two or three days in the fridge with a stopper, though the aromatics fade first, so drink the good stuff on the night.

Buy the current vintage unless you are deliberately after an aged Bandol, and avoid any bottle that has been sitting in direct sunlight. Rose is the most light-sensitive wine on the shelf, and clear glass offers it no protection at all.

What to Eat With It in Late August

This is where late summer rose earns its keep. Pale Provence styles work with cold seafood, goat cheese, salads with plenty of herbs and anything involving tomatoes and olive oil. Spanish rosado handles paella, chorizo and grilled peppers. Tavel and Bandol take on the barbecue directly, including lamb, merguez and aubergine cooked until it is properly blackened.

The one thing rose struggles with is heavy cream and butter, which flatten its acidity. Otherwise it is the most versatile category on any table, which is exactly why it deserves to survive past the end of the school holidays.

Blanc de Blancs vs Blanc de Noirs: What the Labels Mean

Blanc de Blancs means the champagne is made entirely from white grapes — in Champagne, that is Chardonnay. Blanc de Noirs means white champagne made from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, pressed gently so no colour is drawn from the skins. Blanc de Blancs is typically leaner and more citrus-driven; Blanc de Noirs is broader and more red-fruited.

Both terms translate literally and unhelpfully — "white from whites" and "white from blacks" — which is why they confuse people standing in front of a shelf. The distinction is simply which grapes went in.

The three grapes of Champagne

Most champagne is a blend of three grapes. Chardonnay is the white one, giving acidity, citrus and the capacity to age. Pinot Noir is black-skinned, giving structure, weight and red-fruit character. Pinot Meunier, also black-skinned, gives softness and approachability early.

A standard non-vintage brut blends all three. Declare one category on the label and you have narrowed the field deliberately — which is the point.

Four further grapes are permitted in tiny quantities — Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris — and you will occasionally see them in a bottle marketed on that rarity.

How black grapes make white wine

The colour in red wine comes from skin contact, not from the juice, which runs pale in almost every grape. Press black grapes gently and draw the juice off the skins quickly, and you get white wine. That is exactly what happens in a Blanc de Noirs — and it is also why rosé champagne exists, made either by allowing brief skin contact or by blending in a little still red wine.

The two styles compared

Blanc de Blancs Blanc de Noirs
Grapes Chardonnay only Pinot Noir and/or Pinot Meunier
Heartland Côte des Blancs Montagne de Reims, Vallée de la Marne
Body Lighter, more precise Fuller, rounder
Flavour Lemon, green apple, chalk, almond Red apple, strawberry, brioche, spice
Acidity Higher Softer
Ageing potential Excellent — develops nuttiness and honey Good, but generally shows well earlier
Best as Aperitif, with shellfish or caviar With food, or in cooler weather

Which should you choose?

Choose Blanc de Blancs when champagne is the opening act. Its acidity and cut make it the better aperitif, and it is the classic partner for oysters, shellfish and caviar — salt and high acid flatter each other. It is also the style that rewards cellaring most reliably, moving from citrus towards hazelnut and honey over a decade.

Choose Blanc de Noirs when champagne has to hold its own against food, or when the weather is against you. The extra body copes with roast chicken, charcuterie, mushroom dishes and hard cheese in a way a lean Chardonnay cuvée can struggle with. It tends to feel more generous on a cold evening.

Neither is better. They are different tools, and the honest test is what you are eating and when you are drinking it.

Do the terms only apply to champagne?

No. You will see Blanc de Blancs on sparkling wines from elsewhere in France, from England and from further afield. Outside Champagne the phrase still means "from white grapes", but the grape itself may not be Chardonnay — so it tells you less about the style than it does on a champagne label.

Serving either one

Both show best at 8–10°C, warming to 10–12°C for older or prestige bottles where more aroma is worth coaxing out. Serve Blanc de Blancs a touch cooler than Blanc de Noirs if you are pouring both. Use a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a narrow flute — you lose almost nothing in bubbles and gain a great deal in aroma.

Frequently asked questions

What does Blanc de Blancs mean?

White from whites — champagne made entirely from white grapes, which in Champagne means Chardonnay. It is typically lighter and more citrus-driven than a blended cuvée.

What does Blanc de Noirs mean?

White from blacks — white champagne made from black-skinned grapes, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. The juice is drawn off the skins quickly so no colour is extracted.

Which ages better, Blanc de Blancs or Blanc de Noirs?

Blanc de Blancs generally ages longer and more reliably, its higher acidity carrying it towards nutty, honeyed flavours. Blanc de Noirs tends to show well earlier.

Is Blanc de Blancs drier than other champagne?

Not necessarily. Dryness is set by the dosage — brut, extra brut and so on — not by the grape. Blanc de Blancs often tastes drier because of its higher acidity, even at the same sugar level.

Carnival Cocktails: Caribbean Flavours Worth Learning

Notting Hill Carnival falls on Sunday 30 and Monday 31 August 2026, and while the street itself is a beer and pre-mixed can affair, the flat before and the kitchen afterwards are where the actual drinks get made. This is a good excuse to go beyond a jug of punch and learn how Caribbean drinks are actually built.

The good carnival cocktails are not complicated. They are a small set of ingredients used with confidence, and once you understand the flavour logic you stop needing recipes at all.

The five flavours that do everything

Lime is the acid. Not lemon, not bottled juice. Caribbean drinks are built on fresh lime and the difference between fresh and bottled is the single largest quality gap in the whole category.

Ginger is the heat, whether as fiery ginger beer, a syrup made from grated root, or fresh ginger muddled in the glass.

Allspice and clove are the warm spice. Allspice, known as pimento in Jamaica, is the backbone of jerk seasoning and of the liqueur called pimento dram, and it links the food and the drinks of the islands together.

Tropical fruit gives body: guava, passion fruit, soursop, pineapple and mango, all with enough weight to stand up to rum.

Hibiscus, known across the Caribbean as sorrel, gives the deep red, tart, cranberry-like character that shows up in everything from Christmas drinks to summer coolers.

Nearly every drink below is a rum, one acid, one sweetener and one of those aromatics. That is the whole grammar.

Ti Punch, the three-ingredient benchmark

From Martinique and Guadeloupe, and the drink that will teach you the most about rum. Take a thick disc of lime peel with a little flesh attached, squeeze it into a small tumbler, add a barspoon of cane syrup, then 50ml of rhum agricole blanc. Stir. No ice, or one small cube if you must.

It is served strong and small, sipped rather than gulped, and it is grassy, saline and utterly unlike anything made with molasses rum. If you have only ever had Caribbean drinks that are sweet and fruity, this is the one that reframes the whole category. Have a look at the spirits range for an agricole or a good white rum.

Sorrel rum cooler

Sorrel is traditionally a Christmas drink across Jamaica, Trinidad and the wider Caribbean, but a cold version is superb in August.

Steep 40g of dried hibiscus flowers with a thumb of sliced ginger, six cloves and a strip of orange peel in a litre of just-boiled water for two hours, then strain and sweeten to taste with sugar while still warm. Chill thoroughly. To serve, pour 50ml aged rum over ice, add 120ml chilled sorrel and 15ml fresh lime, and stir.

The tannin in hibiscus gives the drink a grip that fruit juice never delivers, which is exactly why it holds up against a rich rum rather than being flattened by it. The base keeps in the fridge for five days and is genuinely excellent without alcohol too.

Queen s Park Swizzle

From Trinidad, and the most refreshing tall drink in the Caribbean canon. In a highball, muddle eight mint leaves gently with 20ml sugar syrup, add 25ml fresh lime juice and 60ml aged Demerara or dark rum, then fill with crushed ice.

Now swizzle: put a bar spoon or a swizzle stick in, hold it between your palms and spin it back and forth until the outside of the glass frosts. Top with more crushed ice to form a dome and add six dashes of Angostura across the top so it bleeds down through the ice.

The swizzling matters. It aerates and chills simultaneously and produces a texture you simply cannot get by stirring. This is a drink that rewards technique rather than expensive ingredients.

Guava and lime daiquiri

A daiquiri is rum, lime and sugar, and the guava version is one of the best variations there is. Shake 50ml white rum, 25ml fresh lime juice, 25ml guava juice or nectar and 10ml sugar syrup hard with plenty of ice for twelve seconds, then double strain into a chilled coupe.

Guava has a soft, slightly floral sweetness and enough body to give the drink weight without turning it into a smoothie. Passion fruit works the same way but needs the sugar dropped to 5ml because it is sharper. Soursop, if you can find it, is extraordinary.

Ginger and scotch bonnet highball

For anyone who likes their drinks with an edge. Make a chilli-ginger syrup by simmering 200g sugar, 200ml water, 60g sliced fresh ginger and half a deseeded scotch bonnet for ten minutes, then straining and cooling. Taste it before you use it, since bonnets vary enormously.

Build 50ml aged rum, 20ml of the syrup and 20ml lime in a highball over ice, top with soda water and garnish with a lime wheel. It is warm rather than painful, and the heat arrives at the back of the throat a second after the lime, which is a genuinely interesting sensation and pairs brilliantly with jerk food.

Batching properly for a crowd

If you are making carnival cocktails for eight or twelve people, batch everything except the ice and anything fizzy. Combine spirit, juices, syrups and bitters in a large container the night before and refrigerate, because a cold mix needs less ice at the point of pouring and therefore dilutes less. Add soda, ginger beer or sparkling water only as you serve.

Two practical points. Taste the batch cold rather than warm, since punch always tastes sweeter at room temperature and people over-correct with lime they later regret. And build it weaker than a single drink, because a batch gets drunk faster than one made to order.

Keep something cold and simple in reserve for people who do not want a cocktail, whether that is a few cans from the beer selection, a bottle from the wine range, or a jug of the sorrel base with no rum in it at all.

Christmas Party Drinks Planning Starts Now

Nobody wants to think about December in early September. That is precisely why doing it now is worth so much. Christmas party drinks planning is one of the few hosting jobs where being early is not merely tidier but materially cheaper and less stressful, because almost every problem people hit in the third week of December is created by a decision they did not make in October.

This is not about buying everything today. It is about making a handful of decisions now so that December is spent enjoying the party rather than solving it.

What Actually Gets Difficult in December

The genuine constraints are narrower than the general panic suggests, which is useful, because it tells you where to concentrate.

Prestige champagne is the clearest one. Vintage bottlings and the smaller houses are produced in fixed quantities, and by mid-December the specific bottle you had in mind may simply not be available anywhere. If your plan involves something particular for a toast, that is the item to secure early.

The second is delivery capacity, everywhere, across the whole sector. December is the busiest month of the year for drinks logistics, and the last ten days are extraordinarily compressed. The third, less obvious one, is your own time. The week before Christmas is when everything else lands at once, and a decision that takes ten minutes in October takes an hour in December because you are making it while doing four other things.

A Realistic Timeline

September and October are for decisions rather than purchases. Fix the date, get a rough headcount, and settle the shape of the evening: drinks reception only, or a full sit-down. That single choice changes your order more than anything else.

November is for confirming numbers and ordering anything scarce or specific. If you want a particular champagne, this is the month.

Early December is for the bulk order, delivered two to three weeks out so you have time to chill and store it properly. The final week is for perishables, ice and top-ups. Note that the ideal is not to have everything in the house by the first of December, since storage is a real constraint in most London flats.

Working Out Quantities Without Guessing

The standard formula holds up well: two drinks in the first hour, one per hour after. For a four-hour evening, that is six per guest, and for twenty guests, one hundred and twenty servings.

Translating that into bottles is where people go wrong. A 75cl bottle of wine gives six modest glasses or five generous ones. A bottle of champagne gives six flutes. A 70cl bottle of spirits gives around twenty-eight 25ml measures, which sounds like plenty until you realise most home pours are nearer 50ml.

The mix matters as much as the total. For a mixed December crowd, something like forty per cent wine, twenty-five per cent beer and cider, twenty per cent sparkling and fifteen per cent spirits is a sensible starting split, adjusted for what you know about your guests. And a genuine non-alcoholic selection should be roughly a third of the total volume, not an afterthought.

If assembling that from scratch feels like work, a pre-mixed case covers the spread in one order.

What Keeps and What Does Not

This determines what you can safely buy early, and it is the single most useful thing to know.

Unopened spirits keep essentially forever. Gin, vodka, whisky, rum and tequila are stable, so buying them in October costs you nothing. Store upright rather than on their side, since high-strength alcohol degrades a cork over time.

Champagne and sparkling wine keep well for months provided they are somewhere cool, dark and free from vibration. Non-vintage champagne is designed to be drunk on release and will not improve, but it will not deteriorate over a few months either.

Beer and cider are the exception. They have best-before dates for a reason, and hoppy styles in particular fade noticeably within months. Buy those closer to the date. Cream liqueurs also have a much shorter shelf life than most people assume, typically well under two years, so check before stockpiling.

Spreading the Cost

There is a straightforwardly financial argument for early Christmas party drinks planning. December is an expensive month for everyone, and buying the spirits and champagne in October moves a meaningful chunk of the cost into a quieter one.

It also protects the quality of your decisions. Ordering under time pressure in the third week of December tends to mean buying whatever is in front of you rather than what you actually wanted, which is usually more expensive rather than less.

Keep the Last Mile Flexible

Plan the bulk early, but do not try to plan every last bottle. Guest numbers shift, someone brings four extra people, and the drink everyone gravitates to is rarely the one you predicted.

Craft Beer Styles Explained, Without the Jargon

Walk down the beer aisle and you are hit with a wall of adjectives. Hazy, west coast, dry-hopped, imperial, session, kettle-soured, Baltic. None of it means anything unless you know the handful of underlying styles those words are modifying. The good news is that there are only about eight families of beer that matter, and once you can place a beer in a family you can predict roughly how it will taste before you open it.

This guide covers craft beer styles the way a brewer would actually explain them: what the ingredients do, how the styles relate to each other, and which ones are worth your time on a given evening.

The one distinction underneath everything: ale or lager

Every beer is one or the other, and the difference is the yeast. Ale yeast ferments warm, roughly 18 to 22 degrees, and works near the top of the vessel. It throws off esters, which are the fruity, spicy, sometimes banana or clove-like aromas you notice in a Belgian beer or a wheat beer. Fermentation is fast, often finished in a week.

Lager yeast ferments cold, around 8 to 12 degrees, then conditions for weeks at near-freezing temperatures. That long cold rest strips out esters and leaves a beer that tastes of nothing but malt, hops and water. This is why brewers say lager is harder to make than stout. There is nowhere for a mistake to hide. A stout can absorb a flaw behind roasted barley; a pilsner cannot.

Stella Artois, Heineken, Peroni, Asahi and Corona are all lagers. Guinness is an ale. Almost everything described as craft beer is an ale, largely because ales are quicker and cheaper for a small brewery to turn around.

Pale ale and IPA

Pale ale is the reference point of modern craft brewing. Pale malt as a base, a clear hop aroma of citrus, stone fruit or grass, moderate bitterness, usually 4 to 5.5 percent. It should taste balanced, with the malt sweetness and the hop bitterness roughly matched.

The IPA is a pale ale with the hop dial turned up and the alcohol raised to carry it. Within IPAs, three sub-styles do most of the work. West coast IPA is clear, dry and firmly bitter, with pine and grapefruit. New England or hazy IPA is cloudy, soft and low in perceived bitterness, tasting of mango, peach and orange juice thanks to heavy dry-hopping after fermentation. Session IPA keeps the hop aroma but drops to around 4 percent so you can have more than one.

Hops are also the most perishable thing in beer. An IPA is at its best within about three months of packaging and noticeably duller at six. Check the date on the can. This matters more than almost any other buying advice in beer.

Lagers worth taking seriously

Pilsner is the classic. Czech pilsner is golden, softly bready and rounded with a lingering bitterness from Saaz hops. German pilsner is drier, crisper and more sharply bitter. Both reward being served properly cold but not ice cold, around 5 degrees.

Helles is Munich pale lager, softer and maltier than a pilsner with much less bitterness. It is one of the most drinkable beers ever made and one of the hardest to brew well. Vienna lager and Marzen are amber, toasty and slightly sweet, the beers you find at Oktoberfest. Bock and doppelbock are strong dark lagers, rich and malty at 6.5 to 8 percent, and are far better in October than August.

Stout, porter and the dark family

Dark beers get an undeserved reputation for heaviness. A standard dry Irish stout is around 4.2 percent and lighter in body than most IPAs. The colour comes from roasted barley, not from strength.

Dry stout is dry, roasty and coffee-like with a bitter finish. Milk or sweet stout adds lactose, an unfermentable sugar, giving a rounder, sweeter body. Oatmeal stout uses oats for a silky texture. Imperial stout pushes to 8 to 12 percent with dense flavours of dark chocolate, dried fruit and molasses, and should be served at cellar temperature rather than cold, in a small glass. Porter sits alongside all of these, generally softer and more chocolate-led than roasty.

Wheat beers, Belgians and sours

German hefeweizen is at least half wheat malt and fermented with a yeast that produces banana and clove notes. It is cloudy by design and should be poured with a decent head. Belgian witbier is spiced with coriander and orange peel, lighter and more citrus-forward.

Belgian ales more broadly, from a dubbel to a tripel to a saison, are defined by expressive yeast rather than hops. A saison in particular is dry, peppery and highly carbonated, and is one of the best beers to serve with food.

Sour beers cover everything from a quick kettle-soured gose with salt and coriander to a barrel-aged lambic fermented with wild yeast over years. Start with a fruited kettle sour, which is bright and approachable, before spending money on anything aged.

How to read a can and choose well

Four things on a label tell you nearly everything. The style name places it in a family. The ABV tells you the weight. The IBU figure, if listed, indicates bitterness, where under 20 is soft, 35 to 50 is a solid pale ale and 60 plus is firmly bitter. The packaging date tells you whether the hops are still alive.

Glassware matters more than people expect. Pour into a glass rather than drinking from the can, and pour with some vigour to build a head, because the head carries the aroma and roughly half of what you taste in beer arrives through the nose. Serve pale lagers and pilsners cold, ales at around 8 to 10 degrees, and strong dark beers at 12 to 14. A fridge-cold imperial stout tastes of nothing.

If you are building a mixed case to work through, cover the bases: a pilsner, a pale ale, a hazy IPA, a dry stout and a wheat beer will teach you more in one evening than a fortnight of reading. Dark Rum vs White Rum: What the Colour Actually Tells You

The dark rum vs white rum question is the most common one in the category and also the most misleadingly answered. The standard explanation is that dark rum is aged and white rum is not, which is broadly the story on the back of the bottle and only sometimes true.

Understanding what colour genuinely indicates, and what it does not, changes how you shop and how you build drinks. Here is the real position, followed by a straightforward guide to which one belongs in which glass.

Colour Is Not a Reliable Guide to Age

Two practices break the assumed link between colour and maturation.

First, caramel colouring is permitted in most rum-producing countries. It is used to make a spirit look richer and, importantly, to keep colour consistent between batches, since barrels vary. A deep mahogany rum may be quite young spirit that has been adjusted to look older.

Second, and less well known, many white rums have been aged. It is common practice to mature a rum in barrel for one to three years and then charcoal filter it to remove the colour while keeping much of the texture and rounded character the wood provided. The result is a spirit that looks like an unaged product but drinks with noticeably more weight and complexity than one that went straight from the still to the bottle.

Add to this that dark, gold, black and similar terms have no consistent legal definition anywhere in the world, and the colour of the liquid is genuinely one of the least informative things on the shelf. What actually tells you something is the still type, the country of origin and the bottling strength.

What the Two Categories Really Taste Like

White rum, at its best, is not a neutral spirit. Good examples carry sugar cane sweetness, a slight grassiness, sometimes a hint of banana or olive, and a crisp, dry finish. Cheap examples are close to flavourless and are essentially vodka with an accent. The difference between the two is enormous and it is the single biggest upgrade available to anyone who makes daiquiris at home.

Dark rum, whether genuinely aged or coloured, generally delivers molasses, treacle, dried fruit, toffee, baking spice and sometimes coffee or liquorice. Barrel-aged examples add vanilla and coconut from the oak, and Guyanese Demerara styles bring a distinctive smokiness.

The practical distinction for mixing is not really age. It is whether the rum contributes freshness and lift, or depth and weight. That is the decision you are actually making.

The Drinks That Need White Rum

A daiquiri is the clearest case. Rum, lime and sugar, and nothing to hide behind. Oak character clutters it, and the whole point of the drink is the interaction between cane sweetness and fresh acidity. Use a white rum with genuine character and the difference is immediate.

A mojito wants the same thing for the same reasons, with mint added to the equation. Heavy oak fights mint and produces something muddled.

A pina colada works best with white rum because coconut and pineapple already provide plenty of richness. Adding a dark rum makes it heavy rather than tropical, although a float of dark rum on top is a genuine improvement.

Anything long and served over lots of ice on a hot afternoon generally belongs to white rum, because dilution flatters lighter spirits and mutes heavier ones.

The Drinks That Need Dark Rum

A Dark and Stormy is defined by it. Ginger beer is assertive and slightly sweet, and it simply overwhelms a light rum. You want molasses depth to stand against the ginger.

Rum punch in the Caribbean tradition, built on the old sour, sweet, strong, weak formula, uses dark rum for backbone, though the best versions blend it with something lighter.

Anything hot, whether a hot buttered rum or a rum toddy, needs dark rum, since heat drives off the delicate aromatics that make a good white rum interesting and leaves only the heavier compounds behind.

Dark rum is also the one to reach for in baking and in cooking, where you want flavour that survives being heated and diluted into a larger mixture.

The Case for Using Both at Once

Tiki drinks have always split the base between multiple rums, and the reasoning holds up. A Mai Tai traditionally blends rums precisely because no single bottle gives you bright cane character and deep molasses richness at the same time.

The practical version of this at home is simple. Take any rum drink you already make and split the base 50-50 between a white and a dark rum. A daiquiri made this way gains depth without losing its edge. A rum and cola becomes considerably more interesting. It costs nothing and it is the fastest way to learn what each style is actually contributing.

Another approach is the float, where you build the drink with white rum and pour 15 ml of dark rum gently over the back of a spoon so it sits on the surface. You get the aroma of the dark rum on every sip while the body of the drink stays light.

How to Buy for a Home Bar

Two bottles cover almost everything. Buy one white rum with real cane character rather than the cheapest available, and one dark rum with genuine molasses depth. Between them you can make every classic rum drink there is.

Check the strength on both. A rum at 37.5 per cent will disappear in a long drink, and 40 per cent is the practical minimum for anything that gets ice and mixer. If a white rum tastes of nothing when you sip a small measure neat at room temperature, it will taste of nothing in a daiquiri too. You will find both styles in the spirits range.

Five End of Summer Cocktails Worth Making Now

There is a specific fortnight at the end of August when the drinks that carried you through July stop quite working. The light goes earlier, the evenings develop an edge, and a glass of something bright and citrus-heavy feels a little thin. Good end of summer cocktails acknowledge that shift rather than ignoring it. They keep the length and the ice, because it is still warm enough to want both, but they move the flavour towards darker fruit, orchard fruit and herbs.

These five are all easy to make at home, all use ingredients you can actually buy, and all give exact measures rather than vague instructions to add a splash of something.

Blackberry and Thyme Gin Sour

Blackberries hit their proper season in late August and are the single best marker of the turn. This is a Bramble variant with the sweetness pulled back.

Muddle four blackberries and a sprig of thyme in the base of a shaker. Add 50ml gin, 25ml fresh lemon juice and 12.5ml sugar syrup. Shake hard with ice, then strain into a rocks glass filled with crushed ice. Garnish with a blackberry and a bruised thyme sprig.

The thyme is what makes it seasonal rather than simply fruity. Bruise it between your palms before it goes in, otherwise it contributes nothing. A juniper-forward London Dry works better here than a floral contemporary gin, because you want the botanicals to push against the fruit. The spirits range covers both styles.

Apple and Rum Highball

Cloudy apple juice is the most underused mixer in a British kitchen and it is exactly right for the end of August.

Fill a tall glass to the top with ice. Add 50ml white or lightly aged rum, 15ml fresh lime juice, then top with roughly 100ml cloudy apple juice. Stir once, gently, and garnish with a thin apple slice.

The lime is not optional. Apple juice on its own is flabby and sweet, and the acidity is what turns it into a drink rather than a soft drink with rum in it. If you want more structure, use a dark rum instead and add two dashes of bitters.

Peach and Prosecco Long Drink

A Bellini is a lovely thing and a poor party drink, because it needs peach puree and goes warm in five minutes. This is the version that works when you are pouring for eight people.

Slice one ripe peach and muddle it with 15ml lemon juice and 10ml sugar syrup in a jug. Multiply by the number of servings, leave it in the fridge for an hour, then strain into wine glasses over one large ice cube and top each with 100ml chilled prosecco.

Using a wine glass over ice rather than a flute is the whole trick. It keeps the drink cold for longer, it makes the fruit aroma readable, and it stops the drink from being finished in three mouthfuls. If the peaches are underripe, use tinned peaches in juice rather than a poor fresh one.

Rosemary Paloma

Tequila belongs to summer, but a Paloma with a herbal note carries into September in a way that a straightforward Margarita does not.

Put a rosemary sprig in a highball glass and press it once against the side with a spoon. Add ice, 50ml blanco tequila, 20ml fresh lime juice and 10ml sugar syrup, then top with about 100ml grapefruit soda or grapefruit juice and soda in equal parts. A pinch of salt genuinely improves it and is worth doing.

Grapefruit is the bridge flavour here. It has summer brightness but also a bitterness that suits cooler air, and it stops the drink reading as a holiday cocktail once the weather turns.

Whisky, Soda and Lemon

The simplest drink on this list and the one most likely to surprise people. A whisky highball is genuinely refreshing, considerably lighter than it sounds, and it is the natural bridge from summer drinking into autumn.

Fill a tall glass completely with ice, which matters more than usual here. Add 50ml blended Scotch, then top with 150ml well-chilled soda water. Stir exactly once, from the bottom up, then express a lemon peel over the surface and drop it in.

Do not stir it repeatedly, which knocks the carbonation out, and do not use a lightly filled glass, because half-empty ice melts faster and dilutes the drink. A blended whisky works better than a heavily peated single malt in this format.

Getting the Practical Bits Right

Three things separate a decent home cocktail from a good one, and none involves expensive equipment. Use fresh citrus, always, because bottled juice is cooked and tastes of it. Make sugar syrup by dissolving equal weights of sugar and hot water and keeping it in a bottle in the fridge, where it lasts a month. And use far more ice than feels reasonable, since a full glass of ice melts more slowly than a half-full one and dilutes the drink less.

If you are making these for a group, batch the spirit, citrus and syrup together in advance and keep everything sparkling separate until the moment of pouring. A pre-mixed case is worth a look if you would rather not shop for five different bottles, and the wine and prosecco range covers the fizz.

WHAT IS BEER?

Beer is a beautifully simple concoction, yet its flavour profiles can be endlessly complex. At its core, beer is the fermented, alcoholic product of water, grains (typically barley), yeast, and hops. These humble ingredients unite to create a symphony of tastes, from bitter to sweet, crisp to creamy. Modern brewing has seen experimental concoctions with ingredients like rice, corn, apricots, and even coffee - evidence of the beer world's relentless creativity.

THE ORIGINS OF BEER

Beer is a testament to human innovation. Its roots stretch back at least 5000 BCE, with evidence suggesting brewing in China as early as 7000 BCE. Interestingly, the invention of beer and bread is believed to be the catalyst for humans settling down and building agricultural civilisations. Beer wasn't just a drink; it was a cornerstone of societal progress.

UNDERSTANDING BEER AND LAGER

Beer and lager - two words often used interchangeably, but what's the difference? In essence, lager is a type of beer. The key distinction lies in the yeast and fermentation process. Ales (another type of beer) use top-fermenting yeast in warm conditions, resulting in a dark, strong drink packed with flavour. Lagers, on the other hand, use bottom-fermenting yeast in colder temperatures over a longer period, producing a lighter and milder brew.

HOW IS BEER MADE?

Beer crafting is a magical process that transforms simple grains into a lively, aromatic drink. The journey starts with malting - heating, drying, and cracking the grains to extract essential enzymes. Then comes mashing, where the grains are steeped in hot water to release their sugars, creating a sugary liquid called wort. The wort is then boiled with hops and spices, cooled, and fermented with yeast. Finally, the beer is carbonated and aged to achieve that distinctive beer fizz we all know and love.

ALCOHOL-FREE BEER - A NEW FRONTIER

Alcohol-free beer, typically under 0.5% ABV, has seen a surge in popularity in recent years. It's created either by removing alcohol post-brewing (dealcoholizing) or by restricting the fermentation process. Alcohol-free beer can even be produced by diluting regular beer with water or avoiding fermentation altogether. It's all about the beer experience - without the buzz. Browse our low and alcohol-free range.

WHAT IS IPA BEER?

IPA or India Pale Ale is a beloved beer style, known for its high hop content and robust flavour, often marked by citrus and tropical fruit notes. Originating from England around 1840, the IPA was designed to withstand the long, hot voyage to India during the British Empire era. Today, it stands as a testament to the adventurous spirit of beer crafting. See our IPA and craft ale range.

WHAT TYPE OF BEER IS GUINNESS?

Ah, Guinness - the quintessential Irish stout. With its deep colour and caramelised flavour, Guinness is a robust and hearty beer, made unique by its thick, creamy head resulting from the blend of CO2 and nitrogen. It's like a warm, comforting hug in a glass.

DARKER BEERS VS LIGHTER BEERS - DOES COLOR INDICATE STRENGTH?

Many assume that the darker the beer, the stronger it is. It's a common myth, but the reality is a bit more complex. While many strong beers are indeed darker, a beer's color doesn't necessarily correlate with its strength. For instance, the Belgian golden pale ale Duvel boasts an ABV of 8.5%, while the dark Guinness only has an ABV of 4%.

WHAT IS ROOT BEER?

Despite its name, root beer isn't like beer in the traditional sense. Rather, it's a sweet, non-alcoholic beverage made from the root bark of the sassafras tree, or the vine of the Smilax ornata. It is made like a beer though, with yeast added to the drink, which is then left to ferment.
