Prosecco vs Champagne vs Cava: What Actually Separates Them

Put three glasses of fizz in front of most people and they will tell you which one they prefer, but not why. That is a shame, because the differences between these wines are not subtle marketing distinctions. They come down to a genuine fork in the road in how the bubbles get into the bottle, and once you understand that, choosing between prosecco, champagne and cava becomes straightforward rather than a matter of guessing by price.

Here is what is going on in each glass, and when each one is the right call.

The Method Is the Whole Story

All sparkling wine starts as a still base wine. The bubbles come from a second fermentation, and where that second fermentation happens changes everything.

Champagne and cava both use the traditional method. The base wine is bottled with a little sugar and yeast, sealed, and left to ferment again inside that same bottle. Carbon dioxide has nowhere to go, so it dissolves into the wine. Crucially, the spent yeast cells then sit in contact with the wine for months or years, breaking down and giving up compounds that read as brioche, toasted nuts and pastry. That is the flavour people describe as complexity, and it costs time and cellar space to produce.

Prosecco uses the tank method, sometimes called Charmat or Martinotti. The second fermentation happens in a large sealed steel tank over a few weeks, and the wine is bottled under pressure. There is no long lees contact, so you get none of that bready character. What you get instead is a much clearer expression of the grape itself: green pear, white blossom, a hint of melon. That is not a compromise. It is the point.

Champagne: Structure and Age

Champagne comes only from the Champagne region in northern France, and almost always from three grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. The climate is cold, which means the base wines arrive with high acidity and low alcohol, and that acidity is the frame everything else hangs on.

Most champagne on the shelf is non-vintage, blended across years to produce a consistent house style. That style is genuinely distinctive: Bollinger leans rich and Pinot-driven, Taittinger is lighter and more Chardonnay-led, Ruinart is famously fine and chalky, Veuve Clicquot sits somewhere confident in the middle. If you have never done it, buying two contrasting houses and tasting them side by side teaches more in twenty minutes than any amount of reading. The champagne range covers most of the major houses.

Champagne is the choice when the wine is the event, when you are serving it with food, or when you want something that keeps developing in the glass over an hour rather than fading.

Prosecco: Freshness, and Plenty of It

Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, principally Veneto, and is made overwhelmingly from the Glera grape. It is lower in pressure than champagne, which gives a softer, frothier mousse rather than a fine persistent bead, and it is usually a touch off-dry.

That combination makes it the better wine for a great many real-world situations. It is what a Spritz is built on, and no amount of champagne will improve that drink. It is what you want when you are pouring for twenty people on a warm afternoon. It works with salty food and with anything fried. Serve it properly cold, around six to eight degrees, and drink it young. Prosecco does not reward cellaring and a bottle three years past its best is a sad thing.

One label note worth knowing: Prosecco Superiore DOCG from Conegliano Valdobbiadene is a genuine step up from basic Prosecco DOC, coming from steeper hillside sites. It is usually only a little more expensive and almost always worth it.

Cava: The One People Underestimate

Cava is the interesting one in the prosecco vs champagne vs cava question, because it is made the hard way but rarely priced like it. Almost all of it comes from Catalonia, and the classic blend is Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada, though Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are increasingly used.

Because it is bottle-fermented, cava has the same autolytic character as champagne, but those Spanish grapes push it somewhere different: firmer, a bit more earthy, sometimes with a faintly saline, bitter-almond edge that makes it superb with food. It is arguably the best value sparkling wine on any shelf. Look for Reserva, which means at least eighteen months on the lees, or Gran Reserva at thirty months.

Reading the Label Without Getting Caught Out

The sweetness scale is the single most misunderstood thing about sparkling wine. From driest to sweetest it runs brut nature, extra brut, brut, extra dry, dry, demi-sec. Extra dry is sweeter than brut, and dry is sweeter still. If someone tells you they want a very dry fizz and you hand them an extra dry prosecco, you have given them the opposite of what they asked for.

Brut is the safe default across all three wines. It has enough sugar to balance the acidity without reading as sweet, and it is the most food-friendly setting on the dial.

Which to Buy, Practically

For a toast where people will actually notice the wine, champagne. For a party, a spritz base or anything where volume and refreshment matter more than nuance, prosecco. For dinner, and for anyone who wants traditional-method character without traditional-method pricing, cava.

A useful trick if you are hosting: buy prosecco for the arrival pour and one bottle of something more serious for later in the evening, when people are seated and paying attention. You will get more out of both. Have a look at the wider wine collection if you are building a full evening around it.

Whichever way you go, chill it properly. Twenty minutes in an ice bath beats three hours in a fridge, and warm sparkling wine flatters nothing. We deliver right across London in 30 to 45 minutes, 24 hours a day, so you can order the fizz and have it cold before your guests arrive.

What Temperature Should Red Wine Be Served At? (Not Room Temperature)

Most red wine shows best between 14°C and 18°C — noticeably cooler than a heated British living room, which usually sits around 21–22°C. Lighter reds such as Beaujolais and young Pinot Noir are better still at 12–14°C. Twenty minutes in the fridge is enough to correct most bottles.

"Serve red at room temperature" is the most repeated and least useful advice in wine. It comes from an era of unheated stone houses where a room sat at about 15°C. Central heating broke the rule, and nobody updated it.

What too warm actually does

Above roughly 20°C, alcohol becomes more volatile and dominates the aroma. The wine smells hot and slightly spirity, the fruit flattens, and any rough edges in the tannin feel more obvious. A good bottle served at 22°C can taste like a mediocre one.

Too cold is a real fault too, just less common. Below about 10°C tannins taste harsher and more drying, and aromatics shut down. Reds pulled straight from a 4°C fridge and poured immediately are muted and angular — which is why the advice is 20 minutes, not an hour.

Serving chart by style

Style Serve at Examples
Light, low-tannin reds 12–14°C Beaujolais, Gamay, young Pinot Noir, Valpolicella
Medium-bodied reds 14–16°C Chianti, Barbera, Grenache, lighter Burgundy
Fuller reds 15–17°C Merlot, Malbec, Rioja, Côtes du Rhône
Full-bodied, structured reds 16–18°C Cabernet Sauvignon, Bordeaux, Syrah, Barolo
Fortified 14–16°C Port, Madeira

The pattern is simple: the more tannin and body a wine has, the warmer it wants to be. Tannin needs a little warmth to feel supple; delicate fruit needs coolness to stay fresh.

How to get there without a thermometer

A domestic fridge runs at about 4–5°C, and a bottle at 21°C loses roughly 4–5°C in twenty minutes. So:

  • Full-bodied red from a warm room: 20 minutes in the fridge.
  • Medium red from a warm room: 30 minutes.
  • Light red you want properly cool: 45 minutes, or 10 minutes in ice and water.
  • Wine stored in a cold garage or outhouse: bring it in early rather than warming it deliberately.

The back of your hand is a decent gauge. A correctly served red should feel distinctly cool against the skin without feeling cold. If the bottle feels neutral — the same as the room — it is too warm.

Never warm a bottle in a microwave, under a hot tap, or next to a radiator. Rapid uneven heating dulls aromatics, and you cannot undo it.

Remember the wine warms in the glass

A poured glass gains a degree or two within a few minutes, faster if you cup the bowl. This is the argument for serving slightly cooler than your target: pour at the lower end of the range and the wine drifts up into it while you drink, which is exactly what you want.

It is also why wine glasses have stems. Holding the bowl transfers heat from your hand straight into the wine.

Does this apply to white and sparkling?

The same principle runs in the other direction — most whites are served too cold. Full-bodied whites such as oaked Chardonnay show far more at 10–12°C than straight from the fridge. Crisp whites and rosé suit 7–9°C, and champagne sits at 8–10°C, or 10–12°C for vintage and prestige cuvées.

If a white tastes of nothing, let it warm for ten minutes before deciding you dislike it.

Frequently asked questions

What temperature should red wine be served at?

Between 14 and 18°C for most reds, and 12 to 14°C for light styles such as Beaujolais or young Pinot Noir. That is cooler than a typical heated UK room at 21 to 22°C.

Should you put red wine in the fridge?

Yes, briefly. Twenty minutes drops a bottle by roughly 4 to 5°C, which is usually enough to bring a warm room-temperature red into range. Longer for lighter styles.

What happens if red wine is served too warm?

Alcohol becomes more volatile and dominates the aroma, so the wine smells hot and spirity, the fruit flattens and the tannins feel rougher.

Can red wine be served too cold?

Yes. Below about 10°C tannins taste harsher and more drying, and the aromatics shut down. A red poured straight from a 4°C fridge will taste muted.

A Practical Rioja Wine Guide: Reading the Label Before You Buy

Rioja is the most recognisable red wine region in Spain and one of the few places in the world where the label tells you something genuinely useful about what is inside the bottle. Most wine classifications describe where the grapes grew. Rioja describes how long the wine was aged before it reached you, which is a far more direct clue to how it will taste tonight.

This Rioja wine guide covers what those classifications actually mean, how the region has changed in the last twenty years, and how to pick a bottle for a specific meal rather than at random.

The ageing ladder, and what it does to the wine

Generico or Joven is the entry level with no minimum oak ageing. Expect bright, juicy red cherry and plum with little or no oak influence. Serve slightly cool and drink it young. It is the Rioja for a Tuesday.

Crianza requires a minimum of two years of ageing, of which at least one is in oak barrels. This is the sweet spot for value across the whole region. The oak has begun to soften the tannin and add a vanilla and light coconut edge from American oak, but the fruit is still forward and lively. It is the most food-flexible tier and where most people should start.

Reserva requires three years total with at least one in oak, and in practice most good producers exceed those minimums considerably. Here the wine moves from fruit-led towards savoury. Expect dried strawberry, tobacco leaf, leather, sweet spice and a longer, more resolved finish. This is the tier for a proper Sunday roast.

Gran Reserva requires five years total, at least two in oak and two in bottle, and is only made in vintages the producer judges strong enough. These are wines of tertiary character: dried fig, cedar wood, forest floor, cured meat, with tannin that has largely melted away. They are also released ready to drink, which is unusual and one of the great practical virtues of Rioja. You are not buying something that needs another decade in a cellar.

American oak, French oak, and why Rioja tastes the way it does

The single most distinctive thing about traditional Rioja is American oak. Barrels of American white oak give strong vanilla, dill and coconut notes, far more overtly sweet-smelling than French oak, which contributes finer-grained spice and a subtler toast. For most of the twentieth century Rioja was aged almost entirely in American oak, and that coconut and vanilla signature is what many people mean when they say a wine tastes of Rioja.

Since the 1990s a great many producers have moved partly or wholly to French oak, producing wines that are darker, more concentrated and more modern in style, sometimes labelled as alta expresion. Neither approach is better. But it does mean two bottles both labelled Reserva can taste startlingly different, so it is worth noticing which producers you enjoy rather than relying purely on the classification.

The three sub-regions

Rioja Alta, in the west at higher altitude, gives the most structured, elegant and age-worthy wines with firm acidity. Most classic Reserva and Gran Reserva bottlings come from here.

Rioja Alavesa, on the north bank of the Ebro with limestone soils, produces perfumed, fine-boned wines with a distinctly floral lift. Many of the most exciting modern single-vineyard wines are Alavesa.

Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja, is warmer and lower, and Garnacha thrives here. The wines are rounder, riper and higher in alcohol, and increasingly good as growers move to older vines and cooler sites.

White and rosado Rioja, which nobody talks about

White Rioja is one of the best-value serious white wines available anywhere. Made from Viura, the unoaked style is crisp, citrus-led and neutral in a useful way. But the barrel-fermented and aged style, which was nearly extinct in the 1990s, is remarkable: nutty, waxy, honeyed and long, and it ages for decades. If you have never tried an aged white Rioja, that is a genuine gap worth filling.

Rosado from Rioja tends to be deeper coloured and fuller than Provencal-style pink, with more strawberry and structure. It is a much better match for barbecue and grilled food than a very pale rose.

How to serve it

Serve red Rioja at 16 to 18 degrees, which in a typical warm British living room means twenty minutes in the fridge before opening, not after. Decant a young Crianza or a modern-style Reserva for half an hour, but be gentler with an old Gran Reserva, which can lose its delicate tertiary aromas quickly. If a bottle is more than fifteen years old, stand it upright for a day first so the sediment settles and pour carefully.

Glassware matters here more than for most reds. Use a decently sized bowl so the perfume has room to develop. A cramped glass flattens exactly the aromatic complexity you paid for.

Choosing a bottle tonight

If you are cooking something tomato-based, grilling, or eating tapas, a Crianza is the right call. For a roast, a Reserva. For a special occasion where the food is deliberately simple, a Gran Reserva. If you are buying for a group with mixed tastes, a Crianza is the safest bottle on any Spanish shelf because it pleases both the fruit-forward drinker and the traditionalist.

Spiced Rum Cocktails That Are Actually Worth the Effort

Spiced rum has a reputation problem. It sits in the cupboard next to the cola and gets treated as a one-trick spirit, which is unfair to a category that carries more usable flavour than almost anything else on the shelf. A decent spiced rum arrives pre-loaded with vanilla, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, allspice and often orange peel or ginger. That is most of a cocktail already built into the bottle. The trick is to work with those flavours rather than burying them.

The other thing worth knowing before you start is that spiced rum is sweetened. Almost all of it. That single fact explains why so many spiced rum cocktails come out sickly: people follow a recipe written for white or aged rum and add the full measure of sugar syrup on top of a spirit that already has plenty. Cut the syrup by about a quarter as a default and you will fix most of the drinks you have ever made badly.

Start by tasting what you actually have

Spiced rums vary wildly. Some are vanilla-dominant and quite soft. Others lead with clove and black pepper and finish dry. A few lean into ginger and orange. Pour 15ml neat, sniff it, taste it, and decide which camp yours falls into before you build anything.

If it is vanilla-led, push it towards coffee, apple and cream. If it is clove and pepper-led, push it towards citrus, ginger and bitters. If it is orange-led, treat it almost like a rum-based amaro and use it in stirred drinks. This ten-second exercise does more for your spiced rum cocktails than any recipe.

The Spiced Dark and Stormy

Purists will point out that a genuine Dark and Stormy uses a specific Bermudan dark rum, and they are correct. That is not what this is. Take 50ml spiced rum, 15ml fresh lime juice, and top with 100ml properly fiery ginger beer over ice in a tall glass. Two dashes of Angostura on top, lime wedge on the rim.

The lime is not optional and is the step most people skip. Without it the drink is sugar on sugar. With it, the ginger heat and the clove in the rum lock together and the whole thing turns crisp. Use a ginger beer with real heat rather than a soft, sweet one, and consider stretching it with 20ml of soda if your rum is on the sweeter side.

The Spiced Rum Old Fashioned

This is the drink that converts sceptics. 50ml spiced rum, a scant 5ml of demerara syrup, three dashes of Angostura and one dash of orange bitters, stirred over ice in a mixing glass for around thirty seconds until properly cold and diluted, then poured over a single large cube. Express an orange peel over the surface and drop it in.

The dilution matters more here than in almost any other drink. Spiced rum needs water to loosen it up, so stir longer than you think you should. Done properly, the vanilla and clove read like a cask-aged spirit and nobody guesses what is in the glass.

Apple and Spiced Rum Highball

An autumn-leaning long drink that works from August through to Christmas. 50ml spiced rum, 100ml cloudy apple juice, 20ml lemon juice, topped with 30ml soda water, over plenty of ice in a highball. Grate fresh nutmeg over the top.

Cloudy apple juice is doing real work here. Clear apple juice is thin and tastes like a concentrate, whereas cloudy juice has body and tannin that stand up to the spirit. If you want to push it further, swap the soda for a dry cider and drop the lemon to 10ml.

Spiced Rum Espresso

The espresso martini has been made with everything by now, but spiced rum is genuinely one of the better swaps. 45ml spiced rum, 30ml fresh espresso cooled slightly, 15ml coffee liqueur, and no additional syrup at all. Shake very hard with plenty of ice for at least twelve seconds and double strain into a chilled coupe. Three coffee beans on the foam.

Because both the rum and the liqueur are already sweet, skipping syrup entirely is what keeps this drinkable. The vanilla in the rum sits behind the coffee in a way vodka never manages.

Spiced Rum Punch for a Crowd

For six to eight people, combine 500ml spiced rum, 700ml cloudy apple juice, 250ml fresh lime juice, 150ml pineapple juice and 15 dashes of Angostura in a large jug. Stir, chill for at least an hour, and only add ice when you serve so it does not water down while it sits. Float slices of orange and a few cinnamon sticks on top.

Make it ahead and taste it cold rather than warm. Punch always tastes sweeter at room temperature, and people routinely over-correct with extra lime that they later regret.

Two more worth trying

A Spiced Rum Sour is 50ml spiced rum, 25ml lemon juice, 10ml sugar syrup and 20ml egg white or aquafaba, dry shaken then shaken with ice and strained into a coupe. Angostura across the foam. And a Spiced Rum and Tonic sounds odd but works well with a clove-forward rum: 50ml rum, 150ml tonic, a wide strip of orange peel and a star anise. Both are quick and both reward good ice.

Building the shelf around it

You need less than you think. Fresh limes and lemons, a bottle of Angostura, a jar of demerara syrup you can make in five minutes with equal parts sugar and hot water, ginger beer, cloudy apple juice and soda water will cover every drink above. Take a look at the spirits range if you want a second rum to compare against, and the pre-mixed cases are a sensible shortcut when you are stocking up for a group rather than building drinks one at a time.

Ice deserves a final word. Cocktails made with the little cloudy cubes from a supermarket bag dilute at roughly twice the rate of large solid ones, which is why a home Old Fashioned often tastes watery by the halfway point. Freeze water in a silicone mould overnight and the difference is immediate.

Scotch Whisky Regions Explained

Almost every bottle of single malt tells you where it was made, and almost every guide to Scotch whisky regions then tells you what that means for the flavour in the glass. The first half of that is legally defined and precise. The second half is considerably shakier than it is usually presented, and understanding why is the most useful thing a drinker can learn about Scottish geography.

Here is what the five regions actually are, what each is genuinely known for, and where the neat story falls apart.

Why the Regions Exist at All

The boundaries are not a marketing invention, though they are often used as one. They were formalised in the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, which recognise five protected localities: Speyside, Highland, Lowland, Islay and Campbeltown. The Islands, including Skye, Orkney, Jura and Mull, are frequently treated as a sixth region in conversation but sit legally within the Highlands.

Crucially, these are geographic designations, not style designations. Unlike a French appellation, they place no restriction on how the whisky is made. A distillery in Speyside can produce something heavily peated and still label it Speyside, because the region describes where the still stands and nothing else.

Speyside: The Dense Heart of It

Speyside is a small area in the north-east, clustered around the River Spey, and it contains roughly half of all Scotland distilleries. That density is historical, driven by soft water, good barley-growing land and, in the smuggling era, useful remoteness.

The house character people associate with Speyside is elegant and fruity: apple, pear, honey and often a pronounced sherry-cask influence giving raisin and Christmas-cake richness. Speyside malts tend to be approachable, which is why so many of them are used as the backbone of blended whiskies and why they are the standard recommendation for someone starting out.

Islay: Smoke, Salt and Iodine

Islay is a small island off the west coast with an outsized reputation. Its whiskies are the ones people describe as medicinal, maritime or like a bonfire on a beach, and the reason is peat.

Peat is partially decomposed vegetation cut from bogs and burned to dry malted barley. The smoke carries phenolic compounds that bind to the grain and survive distillation, which is where the tar, smoke and iodine notes come from. Islay used it because there was almost no wood on the island and peat was the fuel to hand.

Two caveats worth knowing. First, several Islay distilleries produce unpeated or lightly peated whisky. Second, peating level is a production choice measured in parts per million of phenols, so a mainland distillery can make something smokier than an Islay one if it decides to. Explore the whisky and spirits range if you want to compare styles side by side.

The Highlands: Too Big to Generalise

The Highland region is by far the largest, covering everything north of an imaginary line running roughly from the Clyde to the Tay. It is so large that any single description of Highland character is close to meaningless.

In practice it helps to think of it in quarters. Northern Highland whiskies often show a dry, spicy, faintly heathery character. Eastern ones lean fruity and firm. Western ones can be big and occasionally smoky. Southern Highland malts tend to be lighter and more floral, closer to Lowland in feel.

The Islands sit within this designation and have more in common with each other than with the mainland: often coastal, frequently lightly peated, with a saline quality that comes through most clearly in Orkney and Skye bottlings.

Lowland: The Gentle One

The Lowlands cover the south of the country and have far fewer malt distilleries than the other regions, though they are home to most of Scotland grain whisky production.

Lowland single malts are typically light, grassy and soft, with citrus, cut grass and cereal notes and very little smoke. Some Lowland distilleries triple distil, a practice more associated with Irish whiskey, which produces an especially light and delicate spirit. These are excellent aperitif whiskies and genuinely good with food, which is not something you would say about a heavily peated Islay.

Campbeltown: Small, Salty and Distinctive

Campbeltown is a single town on the Kintyre peninsula that once held more than thirty distilleries and now has only a handful. It retains its regional status because of that history and because what survives is genuinely distinctive.

The Campbeltown character is difficult to describe and easy to recognise: briny, slightly oily, faintly funky, with a wisp of smoke and a definite coastal quality. If you have tried the other four regions and want the one that still surprises people, this is it.

Why the Map Tells You Less Than It Claims

Here is the honest position. Three factors influence how a whisky tastes far more than its postcode: the shape and height of the stills, which determine how much heavy character carries through; the casks, whether ex-bourbon, ex-sherry or something else, which contribute a large share of flavour and effectively all of the colour; and the peating level of the malt.

All three are decisions made by the distillery, not consequences of geography. Regional character is real, but it is the residue of shared history, shared water sources and shared suppliers rather than terroir in the wine sense.

The practical way to use regions, then, is as a starting vocabulary. If you know you like a sherried Speyside, that tells you to look for sherry-cask maturation generally, which will lead you to bottles from four other regions that you would otherwise never have tried.

Tasting Across the Regions

The most efficient way to learn this is a comparative flight. Pour three whiskies at once, roughly 20ml each: something Speyside and sherried, something Lowland and light, something Islay and peated. Tasted in that order, the contrast does the teaching for you.

Add a few drops of water to each, which lowers the alcohol and releases aromatic compounds that were previously bound up. Do not add ice, which mutes aroma. And leave a gap between the peated one and anything else, because smoke lingers on the palate and will flatten whatever follows.

Why Is Clase Azul Tequila So Expensive?

A large share of Clase Azul's price is the bottle, not the liquid. Every decanter is hand-made and hand-painted by artisans in Santa María Canchesdá, Mexico, and no two are identical. Add slow-cooked agave, small production volumes and deliberate luxury positioning, and you have a tequila bought as much for the object as for what is inside it.

That is not a criticism, but it is worth understanding before you spend. Here is what the money actually buys.

The decanter is the product

Each Clase Azul decanter is made and decorated by hand. The ceramic is formed, fired, glazed and then hand-painted, a process involving a community of artisans rather than a production line. The signature Reposado bottle — white, with cobalt blue detailing — takes days rather than minutes, and small variations between bottles are inherent to the method.

The commercial consequence is straightforward: the packaging cost per bottle is a large multiple of what a glass bottle costs, and it does not fall much with volume, because hand-work does not scale the way machinery does.

It also explains why the empty bottles are kept. Walk into enough bars and homes and you will find Clase Azul decanters repurposed as vases and lamps. Few spirits have packaging with an afterlife, and that afterlife is part of what people are buying.

What is actually in the bottle

The tequila is made from 100% Tequilana Weber blue agave in Jalisco. The agave is slow-cooked in stone ovens over roughly three days, which is far slower than the industrial diffuser processes used at the volume end of the category, and it produces a sweeter, more rounded spirit.

The expressions differ mainly in ageing:

Is it worth the money?

It depends entirely on what you want from it.

As a gift, it is hard to beat. It arrives looking like an occasion, the recipient recognises it instantly, and the bottle stays on the shelf long after it is empty. Very few bottles at any price do that job as well.

As a drinking tequila judged purely on liquid per pound, it is not the best value on the shelf, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. There are additive-free añejos and small-producer bottlings that deliver more complexity for less money — they simply arrive in ordinary glass. If you are buying for yourself, to drink quietly at home, your money goes further elsewhere.

Both things are true at once. The mistake is buying it for the wrong reason and then feeling short-changed.

How to drink it

Neat, at room temperature, in a copita or a small wine glass rather than a shot glass. Chilling mutes the cooked-agave sweetness that you have specifically paid for. Do not mix it — not out of snobbery, but because the qualities that justify the price disappear entirely under lime and triple sec. What is the difference between Clase Azul Reposado and Añejo?

Reposado is aged around 8 months and tastes of vanilla, caramel and soft oak. Añejo is aged around 25 months and is richer, with toffee, dried fruit and spice, in a more elaborate decanter.

Wine Glass Shapes: What Actually Matters and What Is Marketing

There are companies that will sell you a different glass for every grape variety. Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Nebbiolo, Chardonnay from oak, Chardonnay without oak. It looks absurd, and much of it is. But the underlying claim, that the shape of a glass changes how a wine tastes, is genuinely true, and understanding why lets you buy three sensible glasses rather than eighteen silly ones.

Wine glass shapes work on aroma. Around eighty percent of what you experience as flavour arrives through the olfactory receptors at the top of your nasal cavity, not the tongue. Your tongue detects sweet, sour, salt, bitter and umami, plus texture and temperature. Everything else, every mention of blackcurrant, gooseberry, leather or wet stone, is smell. A glass is essentially a device for delivering a specific concentration of volatile aromatic compounds to your nose.

The three variables that do the work

Bowl width determines how much wine surface is in contact with air. More surface area means faster evaporation of alcohol and aromatics, and faster softening of tannin and any reductive notes. That is why a big Burgundy bowl suits a delicate, aromatic red like Pinot Noir which needs coaxing, while a narrower bowl suits an aromatic white which would otherwise blow off within minutes.

Rim diameter determines how concentrated the aroma is when it reaches you, and where the wine lands in your mouth. A tapered rim funnels aromatics into a tighter column. A wide flared rim disperses them.

Glass thickness has no chemical effect at all but a substantial perceptual one. A fine rim, under a millimetre, disappears against the lip and the wine seems to arrive without an intermediary. A thick, rolled rim announces itself. Blind tests repeatedly show people rate the same wine higher from a thinner glass. That is not a chemical effect, but it is a real experience, and it is the single upgrade most worth paying for.

The glasses actually worth owning

Start with a universal glass, sometimes sold as a Chardonnay glass or an all-purpose glass. Roughly 500 to 550ml total capacity, a slightly tapered rim, a stem you can hold. This handles Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Riesling, rosé, Rioja, Malbec, Chianti and most Bordeaux perfectly well. Buy six.

Add a large-bowled glass of 650ml or more for Burgundy, Pinot Noir, Nebbiolo and older reds. These wines are all about perfume and benefit from air. If you drink a lot of light, aromatic reds this is your most-used glass; if you mostly drink Cabernet and Shiraz you can skip it.

Add something for sparkling wine. A tulip glass, narrower than a white wine glass but wider than a flute, is the best compromise, giving you aroma without losing the bubbles in two minutes.

That is it. Anything beyond three shapes is a hobby rather than a necessity. If you are choosing between spending on a fourth shape or on a better bottle from the wine range, buy the wine.

The pour is as important as the glass

Almost nobody pours correctly. A wine glass should be filled to the widest point of the bowl and no higher, which in a 550ml glass is roughly 150ml, or about a fifth of the glass. This leaves the maximum surface area for evaporation and a large headspace where aromatics collect. If you fill a big glass to the top you have removed the entire reason for owning it and you have created a wine that warms up before you finish it.

Swirling is not affectation. It coats the inside of the bowl with a thin film that evaporates rapidly and refreshes the aromatic headspace. Do it on the table rather than in the air until you are confident, and stop after two or three rotations.

Temperature, stems and the dishwasher

Hold the stem or the base, not the bowl. Body heat transfers through glass quickly, and a white wine served at a well-judged 9 degrees will be at 14 within ten minutes if you cup the bowl.

On serving temperature: most British homes serve white too cold and red too warm. Room temperature as a standard was set when rooms were 16 degrees, not 22. Light reds like Beaujolais or a young Pinot Noir are genuinely better with twenty minutes in the fridge. Full-bodied reds from the red wine selection are at their best around 16 to 18 degrees. Whites want 8 to 12, sparkling 6 to 8.

Wash glasses in hot water with minimal detergent and dry with a lint-free cloth while still warm. Detergent residue kills the mousse on sparkling wine faster than anything else, which is why a glass straight from the dishwasher often produces a flat-looking pour. Store glasses upright rather than on their rims, since resting on the rim both risks chipping and traps stale cupboard air inside the bowl.

Stemless, crystal and the honest verdict

Stemless glasses are practical for a garden party or a crowd, easier to store and harder to knock over. They also guarantee a warm wine and fingerprints across the bowl. Use them for casual outdoor drinking and keep stems for anything you actually care about.

Lead-free crystal is thinner, stronger and more transparent than standard glass, which is why the good ones cost what they do. Whether that is worth it depends entirely on how often you drink wine and how heavy-handed your household is with the washing up. A mid-priced machine-blown crystal glass gets you most of the benefit at a fraction of the price of hand-blown.

The honest summary is that wine glass shapes matter, but far less than temperature, far less than freshness, and far less than the wine itself. Get three shapes, keep them thin and clean, pour to the widest point, and stop worrying.
